candidateRows: God is the transcendent source of existence with whom humans can relate and align their lives, while remaining beyond exhaustive human definition.
This supplies the Jewish-theist side's foundational account of God, religious relationship, purposeful life, and the epistemic limits governing claims about divinity.
After the moderator asks a child's basic question about what God is, Wolpe frames the answer through human cognitive limitation and offers a deliberately minimal relational definition.
God is a human and fear-driven projection that offers paternal consolation, substitutes authority for moral thought, and can culminate in celestial totalitarianism.
The move states the atheist critique's central causal and political account of religion: humans invent gods from psychological need, with authoritarian consequences.
Wolpe's claim that God is the transcendent source of existence and a partner in purposeful human life.
Answering Wolpe's definition, Hitchens contrasts divine creation with the historical proliferation of human-made gods and traces belief from protective wishes to authoritarian danger.
Explaining religious belief through believers' alleged psychological needs does not refute its truth, because motives and the merits of a proposition are distinct.
This directly attacks the validity of Hitchens's projection argument and defends the rational standing of belief independently of any believer's psychological motives.
Hitchens's contention that belief in God is a fear-made wish for paternal protection and moral authority.
Wolpe identifies what he regards as an asymmetry in atheist argument: assigning religious belief to psychology while presenting atheism as the product of logic and science.
A possible first cause is categorically different from a supervising religious deity, and natural explanations leave neither kind of divine hypothesis necessary.
The distinction blocks movement from abstract cosmological speculation to an interventionist religious God and advances explanatory parsimony against both forms of theism.
Wolpe's defense of belief from psychological criticism and his opening identification of God as the source of existence.

Following the exchange about motives for belief, Hitchens separates a deistic creator from a deity concerned with human conduct and argues that cosmic and biological processes work without either assumption.
Consciousness, love, meaning, and the existence of anything at all suggest that reality exceeds matter and can rationally point toward God.
This is Wolpe's principal positive case that experiential and scientific mysteries support the reality of an intangible dimension and make theism intellectually plausible.
Hitchens's assertion that cosmic and biological reality is better explained without any divine mover or supervising deity.
Asked why the source of existence should be divine in 2010, Wolpe rejects laboratory proof as the sole framework and appeals to consciousness, value, meaning, and existence itself.
Modern cosmology and evolution provide verifiable, awe-inspiring natural accounts whose waste, extinction, and contingency are more credible than purposeful religious creation.
The move answers Wolpe's appeal to mystery with a naturalistic account that preserves wonder while arguing that observed destruction and contingency undermine providential design.
Wolpe's claim that immaterial experience and scientifically unexplained features of reality suggest something greater than matter.
Hitchens answers the appeal to something beyond matter by describing a universe arising through physical processes, life made from stellar material, and a history dominated by extinction.
Human free will cannot be accounted for by genetics and environment alone, so genuine choice requires an immaterial aspect of persons grounded in God.
The argument makes human agency a positive reason for theism and directly challenges materialism by claiming its causal resources cannot produce genuinely free choice.
Hitchens's materialist account of human beings and his presentation of cosmological and evolutionary history as sufficient without divine purpose.
Wolpe concedes none of Hitchens's historical framing and pivots to agency, arguing that unchosen birth, genetics, and environment would predetermine action absent an immaterial chooser.
Evolutionary history is contingent rather than predetermined, and its random mutation, natural selection, and testable consequences explain life more powerfully than Genesis.
This is the principal naturalistic rebuttal to Wolpe's free-will premise, denying that material processes are simply deterministic and emphasizing their explanatory and practical success.
Wolpe's argument that material genetics and environment entail predetermination and therefore cannot account for human free will without God.

Hitchens invokes evolutionary branching and the possibility that replaying life's history would yield different results, then points to genetics, medicine, and verification as advantages over Genesis.
Expanding scientific knowledge reveals greater ignorance and therefore calls for skepticism, inquiry, debate, and doubt rather than faith or religion's totalizing claims.
The move directly compares the rival epistemologies at the heart of the motion and argues that faith is both useless for inquiry and dangerous when made a comprehensive solution.
Wolpe's treatment of religious conviction and mystery as non-empirical ways of making sense of an irreducibly wondrous world.

Hitchens credits science with replacing supernatural explanations while enlarging awareness of the unknown, then argues that religion cannot be treated as private because it offers salvation under threat.
Judaism evolves toward goodness rather than inherent totalitarianism, and faith demonstrably deepens meaning, generosity, volunteering, and service to others.
This answers both the authoritarian and uselessness charges by describing an evolving ethical tradition and offering lived and institutional benefits as consequences of faith.
Hitchens's claim that faith is epistemically useless, totalizing, coercive, and among the least useful virtues for real human dilemmas.
After a brief dispute over Socrates and interruptions, Wolpe argues that Judaism prescribes goodness, changes historically, and motivates widespread charitable giving and humanitarian work.
Religious charity often evades the evidentiary case for God while exploiting vulnerable recipients for conversion and supplying false explanations.
This directly challenges the claimed moral benefit of faith by distinguishing secular aid from missionary activity and connecting religious charity to proselytism.
Wolpe's claim that faith motivates extensive charitable work and makes a predominantly beneficial difference.
After accepting private belief that does not seek privileges, Hitchens turns to Wolpe's charity claim, contrasts secular Haiti relief with missionary conduct, and questions scriptural goodness.
Jewish scripture and its interpretive tradition repeatedly direct believers toward justice, moral refinement, and decent treatment of others.
It answers a textual challenge to religious morality and broadens the relevant evidence from the Decalogue to Leviticus, the Talmud, and evolving Jewish practice.
Hitchens's challenge that goodness is absent from the Decalogue and that religious charity avoids evidence for God.
Wolpe cites love of neighbor, pursuit of justice, and the Talmudic purpose of refining character, then argues that Hitchens discounts religious good while treating religious harm as representative.
Religion itself is culpable because biblical moral commands coexist with divinely enjoined persecution, slavery, misogyny, and primitive property relations.
This states a core atheist contention that the defects are intrinsic to authoritative religious texts rather than merely abuses committed by secular or religious institutions.
Wolpe's accusation that Hitchens dismisses religious good but treats every bad act by religious people as representative of religion.

Hitchens denies blaming only religious authorities, inventories excluded biblical neighbors and sanctioned punishments, and concludes that the commandments reveal a fearful, human, property-owning culture.
Religious traditions are humanly transmitted, historically evolving systems capable of refining inherited defects rather than preserving every ancient rule unchanged.
This supplies the principal defense against textual atrocities by denying that ancient provisions exhaust a living tradition's contemporary moral content or developmental capacity.
Hitchens's claim that biblical exclusions, punishments, slavery, and property rules expose religion as a primitive man-made phenomenon.

Wolpe concedes human composition and historical dross, compares moral development to other evolutionary processes, and argues that selective negative passages cannot be presumed permanently controlling.
If faith has distinctive moral value, believers should identify a good action or ethical statement that an unbeliever is incapable of performing.
The challenge operationalizes the central dispute by demanding a uniquely religious moral contribution rather than examples of ordinary goodness performed by religious people.
Wolpe's assertion that religious systems refine people morally and can remove harmful inherited elements over time.
After rejecting the charge of cherry-picking, Hitchens asks for a morally good statement or deed available to a person of faith but unavailable to him as an unbeliever.
Religion can motivate uncommon service and create experiences of sanctity and intimate love that cannot be reproduced without belief in a sacred realm.
This shifts the defense from physical capability to motivation and lived sacred meaning, identifying experiential and motivational goods claimed to be distinctive to faith.
Hitchens's demand for a moral or ethical act that a religious believer can perform but an unbeliever cannot.

Wolpe concedes shared physical capacities but argues that faith motivates conduct people otherwise often do not undertake and makes ritual blessing an expression of sanctity beyond ordinary affection.
Honest acceptance of mortality, entropy, grief, and struggle is preferable to religious promises of consolation that depend on wishful illusion.
It directly addresses the motion's consolation and meaning dimension by presenting atheistic realism as morally respectful and psychologically valuable rather than despairing.
The challenge that without religious teaching society lacks moral structure and no institution will reach people who fall into despair.
Hitchens recommends despair as a starting point for stoic reflection, rejects promised eternal peace, and argues that respecting people requires refusing false consolation and illusion.
Religious community and belief in a meaningful world provide profound, nontrivial comfort amid death and bereavement that skeptical dismissal fails to comprehend.
This is the principal theistic case that faith reveals or sustains meaning under extreme suffering, directly contesting the characterization of consolation as cheap illusion.
Hitchens's argument that mortality should be faced without illusion and that religious consolation disrespects people by offering falsehood.
Wolpe invokes pastoral encounters with dying people and bereaved families, arguing that communal prayer and belief in meaning survive clever criticism when confronted by severe human anguish.
Most wars arise from land, power, resources, and ordinary human aggression, while removing religion has repeatedly failed to produce peaceful societies.
This directly rebuts the claim that violence is integral to faith by offering an alternative causal account and arguing that religion attempts to discipline humanity's crooked nature.
The previously raised concern that violence may be integral to religion rather than exceptional or an offense against it.
Wolpe argues that neighboring groups fight over material interests, cites a small proportion of wars classified as religious, invokes secular regimes, and locates aggression in human nature.
Religion intensifies ordinary tribal conflict by supplying divine mandates, making it a force multiplier in conquest, genocide, territorial disputes, and political violence.
This refines the atheist case from claiming religion creates all violence to arguing that supernatural authorization magnifies conflicts and makes compromise or disobedience harder.
Wolpe's argument that conflict is chiefly material and human, that few wars are religious, and that irreligious societies remain violent.
Hitchens accepts evolved aggression and tribalism but argues that heavenly mandates amplify them, using biblical conquest and modern conflicts before rejecting belief in a partisan supreme authority.
Religious belief need not satisfy scientific criteria, and humanity's recurring discovery of God supports belief as a natural or revealed intuition.
The move directly defends the epistemic legitimacy of belief in God against the charge that faith conflicts with scientific knowledge.
The audience challenge that God would not be inferred without prior religious instruction or scientific support.
After an audience member asks whether Wolpe could discover God without being taught, Wolpe distinguishes religious and scientific assertions and appeals to humanity's historical belief.
Science may coexist with private religious belief, but scientific accomplishment does not validate religion and major scientists have held demonstrably irrational beliefs.
The response concedes coexistence while denying the debate-critical inference that respected scientists or scientific expertise supply evidence for religion.
Wolpe's appeal to prominent believing scientists and his claim that science does not disqualify religious assertion.
Asked whether science will solve everything, Hitchens embraces continuing uncertainty but argues that scientists' private superstitions cannot make science a vindication of faith.
The near-universal Golden Rule is a human ethical approximation whose necessary qualifications show that morality requires judgment rather than obedience to absolute authority.
It supplies the atheist account of broadly shared morality and directly attacks the claim that divine absolutes relieve humans of ethical reasoning.
The audience request for an account of universal morality and its source without relying on religious commandments.
In response to a two-part morality question, Hitchens identifies the Golden Rule across cultures, tests its limits, and argues that ethical thought cannot be outsourced.
God grounds real moral right and wrong while Jewish tradition still requires reasoning; without a divine dimension, evolved interests and power replace objective morality.
This is the theistic side's core account of objective morality, connecting divine reality to binding ethical truth without denying human deliberation.
Hitchens's claim that moral absolutes conceal relativism and that people should reason ethically without absolute authority.
Wolpe answers that Jewish law does not eliminate questioning, but maintains that a divine spark distinguishes objective right and wrong from evolved preference and power.
Invoking a creator to explain cosmic existence produces an infinite regress, and even an uncaused first cause would not establish a personal, prayer-answering God.
The move directly contests a foundational inference from cosmic mystery or first cause to the specific deity asserted by religious faith.
The audience argument that the existence of spacetime and the universe is mysterious enough to indicate God.
Following a question about why anything exists, Hitchens recommends a naturalistic cosmological account and argues that positing divinity neither ends explanation nor proves religion.
Human beings genuinely experience transcendence, ecstasy, beauty, love, and melancholy, but none of those experiences requires or reveals a supernatural dimension.
The move offers a naturalistic explanation for experiences often treated as evidence of faith, preserving their importance while rejecting theistic projection.
The suggestion that Hitchens's appreciation of mystery or transcendence reveals an unacknowledged religious belief.
Hitchens agrees that humans need numinous and ecstatic experience, locating it in nature, art, love, and mortality while denying any supernatural inference.
Religions share the error of privileging faith over reason, while Islam's claims to final revelation and religious government make its present political form especially dangerous.
The response links the general epistemic critique of faith to the debate's harmful-consequences dimension through a specific argument about theocracy and jihad.
The audience objection that Hitchens's book title unfairly targets Islam through a literal negation of a central Muslim affirmation.
Asked why his title echoes a negation of an Islamic phrase, Hitchens says all faiths subordinate reason but argues their harmfulness varies historically and politically.
Atheists can possess personal reasons to behave morally, but only a universal moral order beyond human invention makes goodness binding in every circumstance.
The move refines the central theistic morality claim by conceding atheist motivation while maintaining that objective obligation requires transcendent grounding.
The challenge that Wolpe both denies godless reasons for morality and acknowledges Hitchens's sincere commitment to justice and goodness.
Wolpe distinguishes subjective motivation from moral ontology, arguing that humanly created standards are defeasible whereas divinely grounded goodness remains universally true.
Religious institutions cannot credibly claim to protect society from relativism when secular law restrains their abuse and secular constitutional authority disciplines their doctrines.
The response directly reverses the claim that religion secures morality, arguing instead that secular institutions must teach and enforce moral limits on religion.
Wolpe's argument that morality is securely binding only when goodness is woven into the universe by a transcendent source.
Hitchens cites clerical corporal punishment, institutional concealment of abuse, and Mormon authority claims to argue that secular law and constitutions civilize religion.
Organized religions may struggle, but the deeply implanted human impulse toward piety and enduring meaning will sustain religious belief in changing forms.
The closing move crystallizes the theistic case that religion answers an ineradicable perception of transcendent meaning rather than merely preserving institutions.
Hitchens's prediction that American religious identity is overstated and that nonreligious affiliation will continue to grow.
Asked where public belief is heading, Wolpe concedes institutional difficulties but predicts continuing religion because humans perceive lasting meaning beyond an empty universe.
